Chief Operating Officer
Request For Support – Bedourie Gymkhana Club
 DECISION REPORT

 Date:                                    16 September 2024 Presentation Time: 15 Mins
 To:                                      Ordinary Council Meeting
 Author:                                  Jason Beaton
 Authorising Officer:                     Scott Mason, Interim Chief Executive Officer
 File Reference:                          IX
 Presented for:                           Decision


ATTACHMENTS
    1. Bedourie Gymkhana Club – Community Grant Form
    2. Quotes for Services


PURPOSE
To seek Council approval for a community grant request of $10,000 from the Bedourie
Gymkhana Club to support the provision of ambulance and security services for the
upcoming Bedourie Campdraft, Rodeo, and Gymkhana.
OFFICER RECOMMENDATION
That Council recognises the importance of its community events and approves the Bedourie
Gymkhana Club’s Community Grant request of $10,000 that will be directly used for the
supply of Ambulance and Security services.


REPORT
Background
The Bedourie Campdraft, Rodeo, and Gymkhana is a major local event that attracts
participants and spectators from across the region. It is an important cultural and sporting
event for the Diamantina Shire, fostering community spirit and contributing to the local
economy. To ensure the safety of all participants and spectators, the Bedourie Gymkhana
Club has requested a community grant to cover essential services such as ambulance and
security.
Request
 The Bedourie Gymkhana Club is seeking a $10,000 community grant to cover the costs
associated with hiring ambulance and security services for the Bedourie Campdraft, Rodeo,
and Gymkhana. These services are critical to ensuring that the event runs safely and
complies with regulatory requirements.
    •    Ambulance services: $6,000




Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                 Page 382
    •    Security services: $4,000
Community Benefits:
    1. Public Safety: Ensuring the availability of ambulance and security services will
       enhance the safety and security of all attendees, including participants, volunteers,
       and spectators.
    2. Event Continuity: The event contributes to the cultural and social fabric of Bedourie
       and the wider Diamantina region. The presence of these essential services will
       ensure the event meets regulatory and insurance requirements, safeguarding its
       future.
    3. Economic Impact: The Campdraft, Rodeo, and Gymkhana attract visitors and
       participants from outside the region, providing a boost to local businesses, including
       accommodation, food, and fuel providers.
    4. Community Engagement: The event promotes social cohesion and engagement
       within the local community, fostering a sense of pride and tradition.
CONSIDERATION/IMPLICATIONS
Corporate/Operational Plan Reference/Policy/Legislation

    •    Local Government Act 2009
    •    Local Government Regulation 2012
    •    Diamantina Shire Council’s Community Grant Policy
    •    Corporate Plan
            o Our Community
                    Recognises the value of preserving the unique culture of the area
                    Is enhanced by participation in arts and cultural activities
Budget/Financial/Resourcing
The requested $10,000 grant would be allocated from Council’s community grant fund. The
Bedourie Campdraft, Rodeo, and Gymkhana is a significant event for the community, and
supporting it aligns with Council’s objectives of promoting local events and enhancing public
safety.
Communication/Engagement
Communication has been maintained with the Bedourie Gymkhana Club to understand their
requirements and coordinate the assistance needed.

Risk Assessment
Assessments have been conducted to ensure that all provided and requested support
complies with safety and regulatory standards.

Timings/Deadlines
Approval for the additional in-kind support is required to ensure all arrangements can
be made before the event date 27 September 2024.

Conflict of Interest Declaration
No conflicts of interest have been identified.




Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                 Page 383
Human Rights Impact
The support provided aims to enhance accessibility and facilities, ensuring inclusivity
for all participants, including those with disabilities.

Alternatives Considered
Alternative funding options and support mechanisms were considered but deemed less
effective given the immediate needs and the event's timeline.

12.3.3 DECISION ACTION REPORTS
Directorate: Chief Operating Officer
Heading: Tourism Digital Kiosks and Mobile App
 DECISION REPORT

 Date:                                    16 September 2024 Presentation Time: 15 Mins
 To:                                      Ordinary Council Meeting
 Author:                                  Jason Beaton, Chief Operating Officer
 Authorising Officer:                     Scott Mason, Interim Chief Executive Officer
 File Reference:                          IX
 Presented for:                           Decision


ATTACHMENTS
    1. Specialist Apps - Kiosks
    2. Specialist Apps – Mobile App
    3. Specialist Apps Pricebook


PURPOSE
To seek Council approval for the purchase and installation of two interactive kiosks for
placement in front of the Birdsville and Bedourie Visitor Information Centres. The kiosks will
enhance visitor engagement and provide essential information during and outside of centre
operating hours as well as digitise Council’s Australia Day Honours Lists.
OFFICER RECOMMENDATION
That Council approves the pursuit of external funding opportunities, to cover the cost of two
interactive kiosks for the Birdsville and Bedourie Visitor Information Centres and associated
mobile application.


REPORT
Background
The Birdsville Wirrarri and Bedourie Visitor Information Centres play a crucial role in guiding
tourists, especially during peak travel periods. However, in the summer months, visitor traffic
drops significantly, making it less feasible to operate the centres at full capacity. To provide
continuous visitor services while optimising operational efficiency, it is proposed that
interactive kiosks be installed outside the centres.
Proposal:
    •    Purchase and install two interactive kiosks, one each for Birdsville and Bedourie.
    •    The kiosks will provide essential visitor information, such as:
             o    Maps,
             o    Up to date road information



Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                 Page 391
             o    Accommodation details,
             o    Local attractions and wayfinding and;
             o    Booking services.
Benefits:
    •    24/7 Accessibility: Kiosks will provide round-the-clock access to vital visitor
         information, ensuring tourists can access services even when the centres are closed.
    •    Cost Savings: Reduced staffing and operational hours during low-traffic summer
         months will result in long-term savings, contributing to a quicker return on investment.
    •    Enhanced Visitor Experience:
             o    Wayfinding: The kiosks will offer wayfinding functionality, allowing visitors to
                  easily navigate key tourist spots, accommodation, eateries, and local
                  businesses in Birdsville and Bedourie.
             o    Local Storytelling: The kiosks will feature engaging storytelling elements,
                  highlighting the rich history and unique characters of the Diamantina region.
                  These stories, including tales of pioneers, stockmen, and outback legends,
                  will bring local history to life for visitors and foster a deeper connection to the
                  area.
             o    Cultural Engagement: By incorporating multimedia features, the kiosks can
                  share the cultural and natural significance of landmarks and sites such as the
                  Simpson Desert, Big Red, Bedourie Mud Hut, Carcoory Ruins etc.
    •    Tourism Promotion: Featuring storytelling and wayfinding tools, the kiosks will
         serve as an interactive platform that promotes key tourist attractions, events, and
         local businesses, encouraging longer stays and greater visitor spending.
    •    Australia Day Honours: The Kiosks will be able to provide details of the Shire’s
         honours lists removing the reliance on the physical boards housed in the community
         halls. This information can be updated anytime and provides the options to elaborate
         on the honourees and why they won the award.
    •    Potential for App Integration: The mobile app can extend these benefits, providing
         personalised itineraries, GPS-based wayfinding, and enhanced storytelling
         experiences straight to users' smartphones.


CONSIDERATION/IMPLICATIONS




Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                       Page 392
Corporate/Operational Plan Reference/Policy/Legislation
The establishment two interactive kiosks for placement in front of the Birdsville and Bedourie
Visitor Information Centres is in alignment with Council’s Corporate Plan 2022-2027 long
term goals of:
Our Community
    •    Recognises the value of preserving the unique culture of the area
Our Economy
    •    Flourishes from a growing tourism industry and continuation of major events
Values:

    •    Innovation and Continuous Improvement

The purchase of the kiosks can be offset by a reduction in staffing and operating hours at the
Visitor Information Centres, particularly during the low-traffic summer months.
These savings will be realised by:
      1. Reducing staff rosters during off-peak periods when visitor numbers are lowest,
         particularly in the hotter months of November through March.
      2. Reducing centre operating hours and shifting the bulk of information services to the
         kiosks being mindful to adhere to the require to be open 42 hours per week.
These savings would need to be investigated further to fully understand what can be
achieved without affecting the level of service given to visitors and the community.
Communication/Engagement
A communication plan to market the service to the community and visitors will be developed
when the kiosks are implemented. Additionally, consultation will be undertaken with the
Managers of the Visitor Information Centres to determine the content needed as well as new
staffing options.
Risk Assessment
A risk assessment should be conducted to identify potential risks and develop mitigation
strategies to address them
Timings/Deadlines
Kiosks should be implemented in time for the 2025 tourist season beginning in April 2025.

participants, including those with disabilities.

 DECISION REPORT

 Date:                                    16 September 2024 Presentation Time: 15 Mins
 To:                                      Ordinary Council Meeting
 Author:                                  Jason Beaton, Chief Operating Officer
 Authorising Officer:                     Scott Mason, Interim Chief Executive Officer
 File Reference:                          IX
 Presented for:                           Decision


ATTACHMENTS
    1. DSC - Local Housing Action Plan


PURPOSE
To inform Council of the $12.5 million Scheme Supply Fund announced by the Department
of Housing, Local Government, Planning, and Public Works, and to seek approval to apply
for non-contestable funding of up to $100,000 allocated to our Council.
OFFICER RECOMMENDATION
That Council:
   1. Approves the submission of an application for up to $100,000 under the Scheme
      Supply Fund.
   2. Authorises the CEO to engage necessary resources, including consultants, to
      develop and implement planning strategies to meet the housing needs identified in
      the Local Housing Action Plan (LHAP) and Local Housing Plan (LHP).
   3. Commits to ensuring project delivery by 30 June 2026, as per the Fund’s
      requirements.



REPORT
Background
On 27 August 2024, the Department of Housing, Local Government, Planning, and Public
Works launched the Scheme Supply Fund (‘Fund’) valued at $12.5 million. The purpose of
the Fund is to assist Local Governments in enhancing their planning schemes to better meet
housing needs within their communities. This includes delivering planning outcomes under
Local Housing Action Plans (LHAPs), Local Housing Plans (LHPs), and facilitating housing
outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander areas.
Diamantina Shire Council has been identified as a Group 3 Local Government, qualifying for
a non-competitive funding allocation of up to $100,000. This funding aims to support remote,




Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                 Page 426
regional, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander local governments in improving planning
schemes to address housing challenges.
The fund has two funding pathways – Pathway 1 and Pathway 2

    •    Pathway 1
             o    Is limited to Councils in Group 3 and is a non-competitive, allocation based
                  funding
             o    Eligible projects - to deliver planning outcomes related to endorsed Local
                  Housing Action Plans (LHAPs). May include secondary elements in the
                  projects that result in additional improvements to the planning scheme as long
                  as the primary focus delivers housing outcomes within the funding
                  parameters.
             o    Section 2.1 of the guidelines describe the aims and objectives of the fund.
             o    Applications are lodged using the Departments eGrant Portal – online project
                  proposal form to complete with application
             o    Successful applicants receive funding allocation of up to $100,000
             o    Applications open 29 August 2024
             o    Project to be completed by 30 June 2026
             o    Only one application allowed



    •    Pathway 2
             o    Competitive process open to all Local Governments
             o    Expression of interest opens – 2 September to 16 September 2024
             o    Group 3 Local Governments are not required to provide co-contributions
             o    Maximum Qld Government funding $350,000
Options for Diamantina Shire Council:
After reviewing the LHAP, the following actions meet the objectives of the funding:
2. Planning

    •    2.1 Undertake a Shire Housing Needs Assessment (HNA) to inform planning work for
         housing provision demands across the region for all housing sectors
    •    2.2 Review Shire and local planning schemes to meet housing needs objectives
         while acknowledging the town character, through review of local density aspirations,
         opportunities for secondary dwellings on existing blocks, mixed use development
         options, repurposing unused commercial space, types of construction permitted, and
         any other specific initiatives to address future housing needs.
4. Master Planning

    •    4.1 Consider master planning of identified options to ensure resilient development
         meets community expectation of how town development acknowledges its heritage.
         Planning may be at allotment, street, or locality level.




Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                  Page 427
    •    4.2 Investigate master planning of the provision of future residential housing
         development sites, particularly addressing the provision of infrastructure.
Proposed use of funds
There is opportunity within this funding to include other scheme amendments, if
needed/identified. It is recommended we apply under pathway 1 as it is non-competitive
funding and there are amendments to the scheme that meet the objectives of the funding,
including:

    •   Identifying Rural land or other land that may be suitable to be included in the
        Township zone
    •   Review level of assessment for Dwelling houses where affected by the flood hazard
    •   Review the level of assessment for all housing types (including Dual occupancy and
        Multiple dwelling)
    •   We will also carry out a more in-depth review of the planning scheme to see if there
        are other amendments we could do at the same time.
With regards to an application under pathway 2, we would need to consider further what
amendments could be incorporated that meet the objectives of the fund and develop
business cases accordingly to be submitted as part of the funding applications
process. Pathway 2 Expression of Interest opens 2nd – 16th September, therefore it is
recommended that we only explore Pathway 1.
Benefits to the Community
    •    Address Housing Shortages: The funding will support efforts to address gaps in
         housing availability, particularly for vulnerable populations, including Indigenous
         communities.
    •    Long-Term Planning: Enhancing the planning scheme will ensure future housing
         developments meet the needs of the community while aligning with sustainable
         growth strategies.
    •    Culturally Appropriate Housing Solutions: Working with local Indigenous groups
         will help develop housing that respects cultural values and supports long-term
         settlement.


CONSIDERATION/IMPLICATIONS
Corporate/Operational Plan Reference/Policy/Legislation
The application for the Scheme Supply Fund is in alignment with Council’s Corporate Plan
2022-2027 long term goal of:
Our Community

    •    Has significant private home ownership with all residents appropriately housed.
Our Economy

    •    Is led by Council and the business community, together growing and diversifying
         business and industry opportunities.
Budget/Financial/Resourcing

    •    Funding Amount: Up to $100,000 on a non-contestable basis for Group 3 Councils.



Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                  Page 428
      •   Eligibility: Remote, regional, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander local
          governments.
      •   Application Opening Date: 29 August 2024.
      •   Project Delivery Deadline: Projects funded under the Scheme Supply Fund must be
          completed by 30 June 2026.
Communication/Engagement
Communication has been undertaken with Council’s Planning and Development contractors,
Reel Planning to determine their opinion and capacity.
Risk Assessment
A risk assessment should be conducted to identify potential risks and develop mitigation
strategies to address them
Timings/Deadlines

Introduction



 Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024   Page 432
        Introduction
        This Local Housing Action Plan (the Plan) is developed through a joint initiative involving the Queensland Government*, Diamantina Shire Council (Council) and the Western Queensland
        Alliance of Councils (WQAC) to respond to a range of immediate, emerging, and longer-term housing challenges in the Diamantina Shire.
        This is an iterative process that does not intend to duplicate existing actions of Council or the actions under The Queensland Housing Strategy Action Plan 2021-2025. It seeks to identify
        opportunities, consider an agreed response, develop targeted actions on key priorities and enable ongoing review of effort to adapt and respond to changing need.

        The Plan aims to:
                        1.       develop agreed priority actions to respond to housing need,
                            2.   establish strong foundations for longer-term housing responses to assist housing and
                                 homelessness outcomes in the Diamantina Shire into the future.
                            3.   incorporate existing information and plans that assist with developing responses to housing                      Respond          Identify
                                 need and acknowledge work already completed by the Council, State Agencies, private and
                                 not-for-profit organisations.
                            4.   facilitate targeted interaction between all parties through agreed actions to ensure a focus
                                 on deliverables and projects that can improve housing responses in the short and longer-                     Review                     Agree
                                 term.

                                                                                                                                                            Action
        Approach and methodology
        The plan provides an overview of key community and housing characteristics, and emerging issues related to
        housing in the community and identifies a targeted initial set of priority actions to respond to housing need. It has been developed through a review of a range of supporting
        documentation including:
             •     Regional Infrastructure plans
             •     Diamantina Shire Council Planning Scheme
             •     Relevant Council strategy reports and plans
             •     Statistical data via the Queensland Government Statisticians Office, including Census and other data sets such as building approvals, rental market data, housing approvals
             •     Housing needs data from the Department of Communities, Housing and Digital Economy and other state agencies as required
             •     The Queensland Housing Strategy 2017-2027 and the Housing and Homelessness Action Plan 2021-2025.
             •     Other local data and information such as RAI reports

        Emerging issues and opportunities, key challenges, and potential responses have been developed from the review of a range of data sets, anecdotal feedback, and preceding engagement
        opportunities with Council and other stakeholders.



* The Queensland Housing Strategy Action Plan 2021-2025

 •   The town of Bedourie is the administration centre approximately
     1,600km west of Brisbane, around a 19-hour drive, and 1,193km north
     of Adelaide.
 •   Iconic Birdsville and Betoota are the shire’s other towns. .
 •   The primary industry is agriculture, with the area renowned for
     producing prime quality beef.
 •   The region also has a growing tourism sector, with visitors drawn to the
     region’s history, scenic landscapes, cultural experiences, waterways
     and wetlands, birdlife, and iconic events such as the Birdsville Cup and
     the Bedourie Camel Races.

Key focus areas identified
Areas of emerging concern have been determined through a review of existing data and engagement with stakeholders as identified in the methodology. These concerns will be
considered when identifying and prioritising shared actions.




    Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                                                                                 Page 438
1. Housing Availability
Housing demand in the Diamantina Shire is based mainly on growth in demand for employees. Council staff numbers in Bedourie continues to grow with the additional demand
in services and administrative requirements and seasonal tourism in Birdsville also demands additional accommodation.

Only 8.5% of Diamantina’s private occupied dwellings are owned compared to 63.5% in Queensland. This position indicated that the private housing market is virtually non-
existent, and its town housing stock generally can only be accessed through rental markets.

Occupied dwellings according to the 2021 census represented 56.2% of the housing stock while unoccupied dwellings were 40% (ABS). While this represents a single point of time
over 12 months ago, it may continue to be representative of the current position, however, the percentage of unoccupied dwellings is likely to be less.

The breakdown of housing statistics collected in 2021 was as follows:

    •    Households with families represented 63% of households
    •    Single-person households made up 37%
    •    Detached houses made up 93% of dwellings
    •    Semi-detached dwellings were 3%
    •    Units were 3% of the total dwellings
    •    The average number of bedrooms per dwelling was 2.8
    •    The average number of people per household was 2.1.

The ratio of availability of beds to persons, per dwelling, indicates sufficient capacity if dwelling mix met demand structure. This situation would indicate a focus on the provision
of smaller two-bed semidetached dwellings and units for future housing stock supply, however, Council would still prefer to consider a mixture of housing to encourage families
to develop the community.

The number of dwellings for sale in Diamantina is limited compared to other western local government regions and currently there are no properties publicly advertised available
for sale. Annual house sales over the past decade have been between zero and six (6) houses in the Shire. Only one price was available for a house sold in Birdsville which sold at
auction in April 2021 for $58,000. Council staff are aware of a recent house purchase of $162,000 and an older house for $100,000.

Vacant land was sold in Birdsville and Bedourie in the order of $10,000 to $15,000. There are still an adequate number of vacant lots within both towns. These lots were developed
several years ago but have not been taken up by private investors for immediate construction even though Council offers a rebate of $45,000 on the construction of a dwelling.
There was concern that some lots were purchased by speculators and are being banked. These vacant lots will meet the needs of town growth for many years.

The difficulties in increasing these housing stock numbers can be attributed to substantial costs of construction due to material supply and logistics, and lack of availability of local
house construction contractors across the region. However, Council has a strategy to build new homes for Council employees and sell when they reach the 15-year mark and then
reinvest in new houses to replenish housing stock. Council is the only entity that can accept the long-term risk otherwise the town housing supply will deteriorate.



    Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                                                                                                     Page 439
The current housing stock remains at a good liveable standard due to past renew strategy however, Council has not constructed a house in the past ten (10) years and now wishes
to continue the previous strategy.

Council recently called tenders for the construction of four (4) houses in Birdsville as there are employees waiting up to two (2) years in temporary accommodation. The cost for
a three (3) bedroom house was in the order of $900,000 with only one tender submitted.
Councils have been exploring housing construction types to reduce the costs of construction. Preconstructed and transported dwellings has been a trend to lower these costs,
however, cost remain high. Coordination across local governments in procurement may produce economies of scale, particularly with the house transport.

Housing affordability is still one of the major concerns as there is little to no market competition. Of 8.5% of the dwellings owned outright there are no dwellings owned with a
mortgage (ABS) which may reflect on the ability to gain housing finance in rural and remote areas.

There are concerns regarding financial institutions’ security requirements which include finance applications of up to 50% deposits and large mortgage insurances. First home
buyers cannot enter the rural and remote housing market unless there is a change in policy to allow them to purchase older homes in these regions. They are being penalised due
to costs of new houses being well beyond their reach. Localised financial arrangements to remove these barriers could assist in overcoming this situation.



Response opportunities
    •    Focus on immediate housing responses to the current housing shortage through selective dwelling construction subject to grant funding support.
    •    State and Federal Government review of financial support to provide financial options that are more attractive to home buyers and local house investors.
    •    Lobby Federal Government for first home buyers in rural and remote areas for eligibility to purchase old homes.




2. Rental Market
Many Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Queensland considered to have 'tight’ rental markets are characterised by a vacancy rate of under 2.5%. Over three-quarters of
Queensland LGAs (77%) have vacancy rates under 1% as at December 2021. The current vacancy rate is zero (0) with no available dwellings for rent in Bedourie and Birdsville.
Rented dwellings represent 67% of the total dwellings compared with 33% in Queensland. This is mainly because house construction for rental purposes is financially unviable.
Council is forced to become the main housing provider in the region otherwise there would be no employees to service its community.

The current median rental price in 2021 was $140 per week (ABS). Council rents its housing stock to its employees as well as the public under the Rental Tenancy Authority. The
current rental price for a fully furnished 3-bedroom house is in the order of $340 per week. Council provides a subsidy of approximately 60% for employees only.

As the demand for rentals increases due to single transient employees and permanent staff on fixed short-term contracts, local community members have difficulty competing.
Anecdotally, this situation has resulted in increased rental prices for houses with reasonable liveability quality. Given much of this demand is for single occupancy, employers may
consider as an option, opportunities for promoting shared accommodation thereby freeing up multi-bedroom houses for families. This situation currently occurs with a private

    Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                                                                                                 Page 440
employer who owns several private houses for employees. Unless a person is employed by Council or given private employee housing it would be extremely rare to access a rental
house for other employment.



Response opportunities
    •   Investigate the current rental supply market and the current unoccupied dwellings to identify opportunities to bring additional “hidden” rental supply into the market.
    •   Support for service provider employers to construct employee housing to avoid transient employees monopolising the private rental market.
    •   Continue to review the mix of rental housing types to respond to specific demand.
    •   Explore shared accommodation arrangements for single occupants of multi bedroom dwellings to open opportunities for family household access.




3. Social Housing Supply
There is a high demand for social housing across Queensland and allocations focus on supporting households with the highest needs. The median household income in Diamantina
is $1,792 per week compared to the Queensland median of $1,675 per week (ABS). The total income for 12% of households was less than $650 per week compared to the
Queensland figure of 16.4% (ABS) and the income for 20% of the households which exceeds $3,000 per week is in the same order of the State average of 21.9%.

Low income and supported individuals and families find it difficult to enter the private rental market. When the minimum weekly rent exceeds the target of 30% of their household
income, it is unlikely they can avoid financial stress. Details from ABS (2021 census) recorded that 72% of households in Diamantina have rental charges of less than 30% of their
total income, and there are no households with rental costs greater than the 30% indicator of rental stress. Consequently, this lower proportion of lower income households, may
be reflected in the lower demand social housing stock.

The State manage eight (8) dwellings for social housing in Birdsville and Wirrari manage three (3) social houses in Birdsville. There is currently no registered demand for social
housing in the Diamantina local government area.



Response opportunities
    •   Council and State Government continue to monitor the demand for social housing in the Diamantina Shire.




    Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                                                                                               Page 441
4. Aged Housing and Care
Council rents houses in Bedourie and Birdsville to aged pensioners. It also assists with maintenance of the yards and building. The median age in Diamantina is only 39 years and
there are only nine (9) persons above the age of 70 years that reside in the Shire.

There is a void between aged pensioners living alone in private housing and the opportunity to downsize into community housing. Many local governments have attempted to fill
this gap through the supply of aged pensioner accommodation. However, at times these facilities are required to accommodate essential government employees due to the lack
of availability of standard accommodation. Diamantina Shire has provided some dwellings targeting aged needs however, recent employee housing demand has meant some of
these are rented to other persons.

While Council has assumed the role of aged care support in the community in the void of other housing support, it is one additional service it has taken on which places additional
cost in servicing the community. Clarification of roles in the supply of aged care needs to be resolved.

Anecdotal evidence suggests that government home care packages are providing extended home living for the aged which reduces the demand for special aged-care facilities.
Inclusion of the outcome of home care on aged-care housing demand could be part of a local review, if not already completed by the Federal Government. The difficulty in
providing this support in remote communities will need further investigation.



Response opportunities
    •    Review aged housing and care provision in the region and the linkage to the effectiveness of the stay-at-home strategy delivered though home care packages.
    •    Assess the role of local government in the provision of aged pensioner housing and its impact on Council resources.




5. Employee Housing
To engage worthy employee candidates in rural and remote areas, employers prioritise attraction and retention incentives such as housing. However, housing stock is limited in
these regions, and the standards do not match accommodation expectations from where potential employees are relocating. Relocating employee families away from more
populated areas creates stress within the family unit, therefore availability of a good standard of housing assists in the transition and performance of employees.
Diamantina Shire Council supplies 39 dwellings in Bedourie and nine (9) dwellings in Birdsville for subsidised rental for employees. Council is in the process of adding another four
(4) dwellings to its housing stock for employees in Birdsville.

The trend of single employees is growing, and this reduces the number of family houses available. A mix of multi bedroom detached houses and units would address the imbalance
of use of houses available for families.



    Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                                                                                                  Page 442
Council has a considerable additional cost to service delivery than eastern states by having to supply employee housing. Remote local governments have previously raised concerns
of this substantial cost impost to these communities as they need to divert funds from service provision to supply employee housing. These capital, maintenance, and depreciation
expenses add an ongoing financial demand to already struggling local governments.

The State Government supplies housing for its employees under the Government Employee Housing arrangement (GEH). GEH provides a range of housing types for government
employees such as police, health, and education. They include permanent housing, temporary housing and shared accommodation located on site, such as medical employee
accommodation on hospital grounds and police accommodation on station sites. GEH has provided housing details in each of the towns. There are only two (2) dwellings located
in Birdsville, however GEH have indicated that one (1) extra dwelling is required in Birdsville.



Response opportunities
    •   Consideration of employee housing for single accommodation in managed shared arrangements to allow general access for families requiring three or more-bedroom
        houses.




6. Cohort Specific Housing
The following cohort-specific housing has been identified as an issue to be addressed in housing configurations within towns of the region:
    • Domestic and family violence
    • Disability
    • Youth homelessness
    • Family homelessness
    • Sleeping rough.

There is no specific evidence for the demand of housing for the above-mentioned cohorts, and there is no current provision for such housing. However, Council does own two (2)
2-bedroom units for disabled persons.



Response opportunities
    •   Investigation to be conducted into crisis housing for the cohorts of domestic and family violence and homeless persons to identify the need for such housing.
    •   Evidence of the extent of family and youth homelessness that results in couch surfing and overcrowding should be qualified to assess social housing demand estimates.
    •   Supply needs for disability housing be addressed through detailed assessment demand.
    •   Council to investigate opportunities in the Federal Government National Housing and Homelessness Plan.
    Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                                                                                              Page 443
7. Future Housing Demand
While no specific future housing demand was identified, tourism will continue to grow and impact on housing demand. Council’s economic development strategies will provide
input to future housing needs through the ongoing assessment of the proposed actions in this plan.



Response Opportunities:
    •   Council’s housing and development plans to be linked to its economic development strategies.

OPERATIONAL UPDATE
Community Based Auctions
Diamantina Shire Council (DSC) is coordinating two community-based auctions to clear
surplus Plant, Fleet and Chattels.
Following a quotation process that identified three potential providers, and consultation with
Council at the August Ordinary Meeting, City and Country Realty in Mt Isa was selected as
the preferred auctioneer. John Tully will lead the process and is currently working with the
Executive Manager on a Marketing Plan.
The auctions will occur on Friday 25 October in Bedourie and Saturday 26 October in
Birdsville, commencing at 8.00am in each location.
Council is offering the local community, businesses and stations to participate in the
auctions. Public Notices will be released week ending 13 September. A social media
campaign is also being developed to promote the auctions.
Residents will be encouraged to participate and use the opportunity to tidy up the towns by
removing old vehicles and goods that could be auctioned. Council will assist residents by
organising collection and transportation of their goods to the auction site.
As part of the preparation for the auctions Council has cleaned up the Bedourie Industrial
Depot and has commenced consolidating auctions items.
The Bedourie Stores team have conducted a full audit and stocktake of stock on hand and
identified a significant number of store items that are no longer required. These are currently
being consolidated and catalogued and will be added to the auction items.

separated)

                              PUBLIC NOTICE
                                       Community Auctions

Diamantina Shire Council (DSC) is conducting two (2) community auctions,
in Bedourie 25 October 2024 and Birdsville 26 October 2024, commencing
at 8.00am at the Shire Depots in each town. Council will be auctioning surplus
used Plant, Fleet, Light Vehicles, Trailers, Parts and Stores items.

The community, local businesses and stations are encouraged to participate
in the auctions by offering auctions good for sale. Council is covering the cost
of conducting the auctions and there are no seller’s commissions to pay.
Buyer’s premiums only will be applied to items sold.

Council will assist community members, where possible, to relocate items to
each auction. Auction goods will need to be in place two (2) days prior to
commencement of the auction.

For more information, please contact DSC Executive Manager Brent
Reeman on 0428 197 177.

Welcome

Mr David Wiskar welcomed all in attendance and thanked everyone for their contributions
over the past year. He noted that it takes extra effort to build regional partnerships, and this
discretionary effort was recognised.

David performed a Welcome to Country, and in doing so he acknowledged the
accomplishments of Thelma Green and her son, Dr Ken Green and Alex Wiskar, who is
Ken’s Grandson and David’s Son!

In performing the Welcome to Country, David challenged us to really embrace, understand
and seek out our First Nations history, as it is highly likely that the Census data for Australia,
‘under reflects’ our actual heritage, due to many First Australians not acknowledging their
history in order to make their way in the world, at a time when it was more difficult to be
proud of ones heritage.

This was followed by a summary of the agenda ahead for the day.


QWRAP Program Update

Mr Fenwick provided an update on the QWRAP Program
   • Brief update on the LGAQ, which was formed in 1896 and which currently has 77
      member councils
   • QWRAP
          o QWRAP is an industry-led initiative to investigate regional collaboration on
             water and sewerage services in regional Queensland. The program is a
             collaboration among the LGAQ, qldwater, the Queensland Government,
             through the Department of Regional Development, Manufacturing and Water
             (DRDMW, previously the Department of Natural Resources, Mines and
             Energy) and over 60 participating councils. It provides a formal opportunity for
             councils to consider collaboration and alternative regional arrangements for
             managing services. (https://qldwater.com.au/qwrap)
   • Governance structure
          o Working Group representatives
                  Ms Michelle Bordignon, DRDMW

             o DCQ (Desert Channels Queensland) have shared the draft Biodiversity and
                  Agricultural Natural Asset Emergency Preparedness & Response Plan. This
                  project is funded by the Australian Government Natural Heritage Trust and
                  delivered by Desert Channels Queensland.
             o The plan outlines proposed actions for preparedness, response and recovery
                  actions for biodiversity and agricultural assets with the aim of reducing the
                  impacts associated with catastrophic natural disasters within the region. In
                  recent times, there has been a growing need to enhance preparedness for
                  natural disasters and their impact on biodiversity and agricultural and natural
                  assets within the Desert Channels Region.
             o Key features of the plan include:
                        Identification and mapping of biodiversity and agricultural assets;
                        Analysis of extreme weather events and natural disaster susceptibility
                           data;
                        Preparedness, response, and recovery actions tailored to each asset;
                           and
                        Integration with regional planning documents and lessons learned
                           from recent environmental disasters.
             o Councils were encouraged to review this document and provide feedback

Western Queensland Alliance of Councils Assembly 2024

Welcome

The Western Queensland Alliance of Councils Assembly 2024 was held at the Buchanan
Park Events Complex, Mount Isa from September 4 to 5, 2024.

Diamantina Shire Council was represented by:
   • Mayor Cr Francis Murray
   • Cr Rob Dare
   • Acting CEO Scott Mason

Mayor Cr Peta MacRae, Mayor, Mount Isa City Council welcomed all delegates to the
Western Queensland Alliance of Councils Assembly, which was followed by a welcome to
country by Ms Roslyn Von Senden, a representative of the Kalkadoon Prescribed Body
Corporate.

A video welcome was provided by the Premier, The Hon Mr Steven Miles.


About the WQAC

Executive Officer for the North West Queensland Regional Organisation of Councils, Mr
Greg Hoffman PSM, provided an update to the Assembly.

The WQAC is an alliance of three ROC’s (Regional Organisation of Councils). A
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was first signed in 2020. It was originally 21
Councils, then. The three additional councils are Croydon Shire Council, Etheridge Shire
Council and Mornington Shire Council. A new MoU has been executed in 2024.

The four priorities for WQAC are:
   • Housing, in all its forms
   • Connectivity
   • Roads



Agenda Ordinary Council Meeting Monday 16 September 2024                                Page 452
    •    Financial Sustainability

To find out more about the WQAC, its submissions and publications, check out the website –
https://wqac.com.au/

State election priorities for 2024
   1. Strengthening regional representation
   2. Jointly planning and funding future ready infrastructure
   3. Collaborating to deliver better health, better housing, and better liveability outcomes
   4. Resourcing councils and communities to transition to net zero emissions and develop
       circular economy opportunities
   5. Helping manage seasonal highs and lows
   6. Growing tourism, trade, and 2032 Olympic and Paralympic opportunities
   7. Adopting practical grant and subsidy arrangements

RAPAD US Mission 2024
  • Purpose
        o Better understand and investigate returns for rural communities
        o Strengthen social and economic engagement between regions
        o Connect and exchange international best practice knowledge
  • Learnings
        o Real economic benefit is being returned to rural and remote communities
        o Texas offers a model for development which will allow RAPAD to emulate and
           learn from
        o Such developments do diversify rural and remote communities economies
           away from the weather by developing additional economic income streams
        o Landholders and communities need to proactively ensure the best outcomes
           when dealing with developers, especially regarding issues like
           decommissioning of sites
        o Communities and councils must ensure they are ready for development. Be
           prepared to maximise this opportunity by ensuring residential and industrial
           planning is well underway to make best use of the opportunity
        o Whilst such investment in energy infrastructure will assist rural communities
           diversify their economies it is not a silver bullet to long-term issues like
           depopulation
        o It can help by providing a ‘third leg’ to the stool by adding to, not replacing,
           existing industries (agriculture and tourism)
  • Success looks like
        o Economic uplift for the region long term, not just a ‘sugar hit’ of construction
        o A more diversified economy that builds on our existing industries
        o Genuine community benefit from developed ‘rules of engagement’ with
           developers
        o A reinforced grid delivering more reliable power
  • An MoU has been signed between Sweetwater Enterprise for Economic
     Development, Texas and RAPAD
  • RAPAD Power Grid - https://www.rapadpowergrid.com.au/
